title: Complexity, Ordering and Equality Contracts
learningObjectives: Compare expected operation costs for common collection implementations
Explain average lookup behavior for hash-based collections
Describe logarithmic lookup behavior for tree-based collections
Maintain the equals and hashCode contract for value-based objects
Use comparator tie-breakers when distinct values need distinct ordering

understand.concept: Hash-based collections rely on consistent equals and hashCode; sorted collections rely on comparison. Big-O describes growth, not exact elapsed time.
understand.whyItMatters: Complexity, Ordering and Equality Contracts helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Complexity describes growth

Algorithmic complexity describes how resource use grows as input size grows. Big-O notation is an asymptotic description, not a stopwatch prediction for a particular machine. Constant factors, data distribution, memory locality, resizing, collisions and workload all affect observed performance.

## Common collection trade-offs

ArrayList provides constant-time indexed access in typical analysis; inserting or removing near the beginning can require shifting later elements. LinkedList indexed access requires traversal, even though insertion or removal at a known node can be efficient. HashMap and HashSet commonly provide expected constant-time basic operations with well-distributed hashes, but this is not an unconditional worst-case guarantee. TreeMap and TreeSet provide sorted traversal and logarithmic-time basic operations.

## Equality and hashing

Hash-based collections use hashCode to select candidate buckets and equals to distinguish keys or elements. The contract requires that equal objects have equal hash codes. Unequal objects may share a hash code. If a field used by equals/hashCode changes while an object is a key in a HashMap or member of a HashSet, lookup behavior can become surprising; prefer stable key state.

## Ordering and comparison

Sorted collections use natural ordering or a Comparator. For TreeSet and TreeMap, compare returning zero means the values are equivalent for set membership or map-key identity, even if equals returns false. Make comparison consistent with equals where practical, or clearly document the intended difference. Add tie-breaker fields when distinct values must remain distinct in a sorted set.

## Measure the real workload

Choose based on required semantics first, then expected operation frequency and scale. Use benchmarks for performance questions rather than assuming Big-O alone predicts latency. Test duplicates, collisions, missing keys, equal-but-distinct objects and comparator ties.

examples.title: Hash-based lookup and equality
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { record User(int id, String name) {} java.util.Map<Integer,User> users = new java.util.HashMap<>(); users.put(7, new User(7, "Asha")); System.out.println(users.get(7).name()); } }
examples.explanation: HashMap offers expected constant-time lookup under suitable hash distribution; this example retrieves the User associated with key 7.

examples.title: Sorted-map lookup
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { java.util.Map<Integer,String> users = new java.util.TreeMap<>(); users.put(3, "C"); users.put(1, "A"); users.put(2, "B"); System.out.println(users.keySet()); } }
examples.explanation: TreeMap keeps keys sorted and its basic lookup operations have logarithmic-time complexity.

examples.title: equals and hashCode consistency
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { record Product(String code) {} java.util.Set<Product> products = new java.util.HashSet<>(); products.add(new Product("PEN")); products.add(new Product("PEN")); System.out.println(products.size()); } }
examples.explanation: Record-generated equals and hashCode use the record components, so two Product records with the same code compare equal and the set stores one distinct value.

examples.title: Comparator tie-breaker
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { record Person(String name, int age) {} java.util.Comparator<Person> order = java.util.Comparator.comparingInt(Person::age).thenComparing(Person::name); java.util.Set<Person> people = new java.util.TreeSet<>(order); people.add(new Person("Mira", 20)); people.add(new Person("Asha", 20)); System.out.println(people.size()); } }
examples.explanation: The comparator uses age and then name. The second comparison breaks the age tie, so both people remain distinct in the TreeSet.

examples.title: Indexed access trade-off
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { java.util.List<Integer> values = new java.util.ArrayList<>(java.util.List.of(10,20,30)); System.out.println(values.get(2)); } }
examples.explanation: ArrayList supports constant-time indexed access in typical analysis, so get(2) retrieves the third element directly.

practise.guidedTask: Implement a value class that correctly overrides equals and hashCode. Add two equal instances to a HashSet and confirm only one logical value remains.
practise.independentTask: Compare lookup in HashMap and TreeMap using a representative dataset. Explain average versus logarithmic complexity without claiming fixed elapsed times.
hints: Use Big-O to compare growth trends, not to claim an exact runtime on every machine.
For hash collections, equal objects must have equal hash codes; keep fields used by equals/hashCode stable while stored as keys or set members.
For TreeSet and TreeMap, compare returning zero defines ordering equivalence; add tie-breakers if distinct records must remain distinct.
practise.challenge: Create a comparator that compares only a person's age and show how equal ages affect TreeSet uniqueness; revise it with a tie-breaker.

questions.prompt: What is the expected average lookup complexity often associated with HashMap?
questions.explanation: HashMap is commonly described as expected O(1) for basic lookup when hash codes are well distributed; collisions and implementation details affect worst cases.

questions.prompt: What is the typical lookup complexity of TreeMap?
questions.explanation: TreeMap is backed by a balanced search tree, giving logarithmic-time basic lookup, insertion and removal.

questions.prompt: What contract must hashCode follow with equals?
options: Equal objects must have equal hash codes
Unequal objects must always have different hash codes
hashCode must return a positive number
equals must compare object identity only
questions.answer: Equal objects must have equal hash codes
questions.explanation: The equals/hashCode contract requires equal objects to produce the same hash code; unequal objects are allowed to collide.

options: How resource usage grows with input size
Exact execution time on every computer
questions.answer: How resource usage grows with input size
questions.explanation: Big-O describes asymptotic growth in resource use as input size increases, not exact wall-clock time on every computer.

questions.prompt: What does a Comparator returning zero indicate in a sorted set?
options: The compared values are equivalent for ordering and uniqueness
questions.answer: The compared values are equivalent for ordering and uniqueness
questions.explanation: In a sorted set, compare returning zero means the elements occupy the same ordering position and are treated as duplicates by the set.
